content.title: '#SKYKING' revisits Richard Russell’s 2018 SeaTac plane theft and 73-minute flight
content.text: PORTLAND, Ore. (KATU) — A new documentary film, #SKYKING, revisits the life and death of Richard “Beebo” Russell, a ground service agent at SeaTac Airport who stole a $33 million airplane and flew it around the skies of Seattle.The documentary debuted on Hulu today, April 14.Director and producer Patricia E. Gillespie said the film centers on Russell clocking into work one day “wearing a shirt that says 'the sky is no limit'” before taking the plane and “joy rode it around the skies of Seattle.” She said she was drawn to the story after hearing snippets of Russell’s conversations with the FAA that were circulating online around the time of the 2018 incident.“The complete recordings weren’t available, but there was a decent amount of his this exchange just floating around on social media,” Gillespie said.On August 10, 2018, Richard Russell, a Horizon Air ground service agent, stole a Dash 8-400 aircraft from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. Over the next seventy-one minutes, Russell flew around the Puget Sound area before crashing the plane on a remote island. A new documentary takes us behind the scenes of that fateful day and we hear from family and friends of Richard Russel. "SkyKing - Panic in the sky" debuts on April 14 on Hulu - ABC News Studios frameShe said she recognized something familiar in Russell’s voice because she also grew up working class. She described it as “this sweet, apologetic, almost a tense funny voice” that didn’t match what she expected to hear from someone who had stolen a plane.Gillespie said the film aims to present a broad range of perspectives, including voices from the FAA, Russell’s colleagues, his family and a “citizen archive” that reflects public reaction, including fear and concern. “What he did was certainly dangerous and his family doesn’t mince words about that,” she said.Rather than trying to “balance or curate or decide,” Gillespie said her approach was to listen and build a cross section of voices. “It’s sometimes better to be curious than it is to rush to judgment,” she said.Gillespie said the production process began with audio heard out of context and expanded as she and her team worked to obtain original FAA recordings. She noted her husband is an archive producer, and together they were able to pursue the material over time while working other jobs. She said the filmmakers were able to share the full recordings with Russell’s family for the first time, calling that experience “really powerful.”The film also includes at least one co-worker, Andreas, who Gillespie said felt comfortable speaking after moving on from the job. She said she spoke with many of Russell’s co-workers, though not all were willing to come forward. Gillespie said Andreas “really wanted to tell the world who he knew his friend to be, which was very different than the picture that was painted in media.”Gillespie said one of the biggest lessons from making the film was how quickly online narratives can harden before key details are understood. She said the internet moved fast to decide “who he was and what he meant,” and that the result was missing both the human story and what she described as an important class story at the heart of the incident.On August 10, 2018, Richard Russell, a Horizon Air ground service agent, stole a Dash 8-400 aircraft from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. Over the next seventy-one minutes, Russell flew around the Puget Sound area before crashing the plane on a remote island. A new documentary takes us behind the scenes of that fateful day and we hear from family and friends of Richard Russel. "SkyKing - Panic in the sky" debuts on April 14 on Hulu - ABC News Studios frameThe film does not claim a single cause for what happened, the director and producer said, but it does explore the intersection of class, men and mental health.Gillespie said the film also addresses how the story was sometimes glorified online and said it was important to include Russell’s family to avoid that and “hopefully reverse some of it.”“As most people know, this story ends tragically. He dies. He ends his life,” she said. Gillespie said the film highlights the impact of suicide not only on the person who dies but also on the people who care about them.Gillespie also pushed back on the idea that Russell’s comments about wages were minor. She said his remark was “not a passing comment,” describing it as “an affirmative clear statement where he said, ‘If you ask me why I did it.’” She said she hopes viewers will listen to it again “in context” through the film.While questions have persisted about airport security, how Russell was able to get the aircraft off the runway, and why he was in the air for 73 minutes, Gillespie said the documentary’s focus is less on “the mechanics of a theft” and more on what Russell represented to people and what may have led to the incident. She said the film raises broader questions, including why there wasn’t a hostage negotiator or a therapist on call, and she hopes it prompts productive conversation about how public institutions like the FAA and airports work.
